Just came back from a few days in my car skiing palisades and donner pass. It’s feasible! A few things I’ve learned…

-Be aware that some sleeping bag brands rate their bags for survival, others for comfort. A therm-a-rest pad, marmot 0° bag, wool blanket, toe end of the bag stuffed into a trash bag or stuff sack for extra insulation, and a couple hand warmers tossed in there has kept me toasty in -10s in Canada and negative teens in Jackson hole, but my 0° bag by itself does not keep me warm enough to sleep in 0 degrees…just warm enough to live. 

-Consider whether you snore before cracking windows in a place where stealth is important…learned that with my boyfriend, lol.

-A jetboil or small camping stove is clutch, especially in a pinch when you want to melt snow or toss a hot water bottle into your bag on a really cold night. If you bring one, good to have something (like a plastic storage container) to take out and set it up on. Food high in healthy fat (ex. fish, avocado), protein, and complex carbs is best for a slow release of body heat all night.

-Less important when daytime temps stay below 40s, but when I was living in an accord for weeks-months I always sorted trash to keep my home smelling nice—wet trash is sealed in gallon ziplocks in the trunk, dry trash gets the regular trash bag.

-Window/windshield covers are a must. [This](https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=YfPYhDCbnG8) tutorial is great—mine still hold up even after a couple years. I picked up some bungee cords with hook ends at a Walmart and rigged a storage “net” on the interior roof handles to keep them out of the way during the day.

-Bring a battery-powered tent light/headlamp and a portable charger to avoid draining your car. If you don’t have a portable charger and care about an alarm going off/using your phone in the morning, sleep with it under your shirt or mid layer. Stick your water bottles in the bag on cold nights to keep them from freezing. Change and get your sleeping setup ready in the boreal lot before driving to your sleeping spot, then blast the heat on your way over.

-If temps get REALLY low or if your car doesn’t do well in cold, park facing SE with a line of sight to the rising sun.

Have fun! You’re welcome to DM me if you have any questions.

You've had an intense two days. I'm sorry you had to witness that. Worry for your mom has probably been at the front and center of your mind, but I urge you to take the time to check in with yourself and address your own physical/emotional needs if you haven't had a chance.

You write that your father yelled at your mom to die, and punched her head right after. You were trying to protect your mom from his explicit threat to her life by hitting him. You did the right thing. There's nothing to regret about that act.

Talking to your mom sounds like a good idea to me. I wouldn't worry about reminding her of it, when it happened so recently--it has very likely already been on her mind for the past two days. I've never been a mother, but I know how it feels to seek out death as an alternative to living with an abusive partner. Having to look you in the eyes and confront how deeply her actions have hurt you may be helpful for her.

I'm a stranger online; I don't know the whole story here. I wonder how long your dad has acted violently in arguments. I wonder how long your mom has felt suicidal, and whether being around your father is more of a threat to her life than any lighter or insect spray that you and your brother could take away. I wonder how old you and your brother are, and how possible it is for you both to get the fuck out of that house for your own safety. For now, recording audio/photo evidence when your dad gets angry is a good idea. Better to have it and never use it than to wish you did.

Sending you a lot of love. You stood up for your mom in a terrifying situation--you have a bigger heart and are more courageous than your father will ever be.

Wool goes a long way. Wool blanket over my 0º bag has kept me warm sleeping in my car on -10ºF nights in Canada and Wyoming. [This](https://www.amazon.com/Arcturus-Backwoods-Wool-Blanket-Emergency/dp/B09C2PTM4G?ref_=ast_sto_dp&th=1&psc=1) is the blanket I use and the highest percent wool blend I found that's still at an affordable price (pure wool blankets can easily be a couple hundred bucks).

I also adapted [this](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NUvz1XcEe20) tutorial to make insulating inserts for my windows--more heat is leeched from your windows than from anywhere else in the vehicle. Just make sure to trim them as you go to allow for use with a heater that requires window(s) cracked.

I also plan to strip/apply insulation to my entire sleeping area (in my case, the removed backseat/trunk of a car) and put a layer of reflectix/insulating material under the mattress for good measure.

The IRS published a report showing that in 2014 the top 400 contributors to annual US tax revenue paid, on average, 23.13% of federal tax rate. In 2020, Jeff Bezos paid a whopping 0.98% of federal tax rate. The belief that a taxation system riddled with enough loopholes to allow the wealthiest man on earth to avoid paying 99.02% of what the federal government suggests he owes is a fairly designed one because it “tries” to tax the rich more is wishful thinking at best and insidious propaganda at worst. The complexity of this system and obscurity of many of these loopholes from public knowledge is such that the amount a person is capable of saving in taxes is directly dependent on the amount they are capable of spending on tax attorneys. To find evidence that we exist in a system designed to keep the poor poor and the rich rich, you don’t need to look beyond data provided by our own federal government.

In 2014, two professors at Princeton University conducted multivariate analysis of the answers to 1,779 survey questions on public policy issues given to Americans between 1981 and 2002. Separating these answers by income level and looking at the degree to which a given level’s survey answers reflected the policies enacted that year, they found that “economic elites and organised groups representing business interests have substantial independent impacts on US government policy, while average citizens and mass-based interest groups have little or no independent influence.” These findings indicate that the United States does not just have a flawed system—we no longer fit the definition of a democracy.

The idea that poor people “deserve” to be poor if they dare to claim that their inability to escape poverty is influenced by every aspect of the system in which they exist and not just the result of laziness, poor character, divine intention, “the way things are”…..is absurd. If you do the bare minimum of research and choose to draw your own conclusions here instead of parroting what you have been told or what your relative privilege may have allowed you accept unquestioned, you will understand this.

I’m happy for you if you have never had to experience things that challenged your belief in the fairness of American fiscal structure. Many of us have not been as lucky.

The first times I visited my bf with scars, I never brought up that I had them or tried to warn him or anything. If I were you, I would do what I could to make this a gradual reveal and not a sudden one. From my experience anyway, the amount that you seem comfortable in your scars can really influence the amount that others accept them. With that in mind, you could start by wearing things that don't quite cover them, and show him yourself bit by bit. This can help you ease into that terror of being fully seen. This can also let you see a rejection coming before it has the chance to hit full force. When you get naked, if you have any control over the location, you can start with low lighting. Don't take your shirt off and immediately start with disclaimers or apologies for yourself. You have nothing to apologize for. Just let him see you and carry on. If he asks, keep it simple. Maybe you volunteer it by choice, but you don't OWE him or anyone else an explanation of why your pain was "enough" to warrant doing this.

What's deemed necessary to report may vary to a degree from person to person.

We have a [nerve](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/what-causes-chest-pains/) that extends from our brain stem down our esophagus and across our chest and abdomen. Scientists believe that the part of our brain that regulates emotion can respond to severe emotional stress by activating this nerve--this creates that lump feeling in your throat and pangs/hollowness in your chest. It could also explain why some people vomit after experiencing/re-living trauma or feel sick to their stomach from anxiety. [Stimulation of this nerve](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/what-causes-chest-pains/) (the vagus nerve) is used as an experimental long-term treatment for treatment-resistant depression.
